title: Construction Procurement: How to Vet Subcontractor Scope Before Award

## Subs Are Getting Faster at Protecting Themselves


Something has shifted in subcontractor behavior over the last few years. The unspoken gentleman's agreement — "we'll figure it out in the field" — is disappearing.


As one Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC put it: *"We have less subs who just go with a gentleman's agreement. They've become more quick to clarify that they're not including that one piece of scope."*


That's not a complaint. That's a warning. If subs are tightening their exclusions, GC procurement teams need a faster, more rigorous way to catch the gaps before award.


Because once the subcontract is signed, the gap is your problem.


## Where Scope Gaps Enter the Project


Scope gaps don't appear randomly. They follow predictable patterns — and most originate in procurement, not construction.


Here are the three most common entry points:


### 1. Bids That Don't Align to a Detailed Scope Package


When you send bid documents without a structured, trade-specific scope of work, every sub fills in the blanks differently. One includes concrete pumping. One excludes it. You can't see the difference until you're comparing apples to bowling balls.


The fix isn't to call every sub. It's to define the scope clearly before bids come in — and compare against that definition at award.


### 2. Scope Sheets That Aren't Drawn From the Documents


The most common anti-pattern in pre-construction is writing scope from memory or last project's template instead of the current drawing set and specification book.


"As per plans and specs" is the line that causes the most disputes. It sounds complete. It isn't. It shifts responsibility but doesn't confirm coverage.


A Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC described what detailed scoping actually requires: *"It's descriptive — bread, put it on a plate, use the open jar. You have to get to that level of detail or else they'll just be like, 'you didn't tell us that.'"*


### 3. The Five-Minutes-Before-Bid Review


Procurement is fast. Award deadlines are real. When a 2,000-page specification book lands on an estimator's desk three days before award, the review is surface-level at best.


That's not a people problem. It's a process problem. The documents are too big and the window is too short.


## What a Proper Pre-Award Scope Review Covers


A complete pre-award scope review does three things:


1. **Confirms coverage** — every item in the project set is assigned to a trade, with no white space between scopes.
2. **Flags drawing conflicts** — civil, structural, and architectural drawings don't always agree. Those conflicts need to be identified before award, not discovered during installation.
3. **Matches sub bids to a defined scope** — so you're comparing each quote against the same baseline, not guessing what each sub included.


The problem is that doing all three properly takes time most procurement teams don't have. A thorough manual review of a mid-size commercial project can take 30 to 40 hours per bid.


That's one person, one week, on one pursuit.


## The Dollar Cost of Getting It Wrong


These aren't hypothetical risks. They're line items from real projects.


- A **$300,000 scope gap** on lead-lined glass for a hospital imaging suite. The GC absorbed it under "readily inferable" contract language.
- A **$400,000 missed roof cover board** on a $50M project. Recovered only through a relational concession from the sub — not through contract.
- A **$200,000 wood-flooring gap** on a luxury condo that no one caught until buyout.
- A **$45,000 stone-depth mismatch** between civil/structural and architectural drawings on a single slab.


These examples come from Provision's research across 200+ GC interviews, documented in[The Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook/trade-specific-scope-gaps) . The pattern is consistent: the gap was visible in the documents. No one had time to find it.


According to a 2018 study by PlanGrid and FMI, poor project data and communication breakdowns together drove nearly half of all rework costs in the U.S. construction industry — totaling $31.3 billion that year. The root cause wasn't execution. It was incomplete scope definition upstream.


## Trade-Specific Scope Risks Procurement Should Watch


Some trades generate scope disputes more often than others. A procurement team doing pre-award review should apply extra scrutiny to these areas:


### MEP


Motor starters, fire-rated louvres, lighting controls, generator field conditioning — these items appear in multiple spec sections and fall through the cracks between trades. Ask explicitly: who owns each of these? Get it in writing before award.


### Envelope and Roofing


Roof cover board, masonry-storefront flashings, and caulking responsibilities (interior vs. exterior) are frequently disputed. The sub's bid may exclude items that the drawings clearly show as in scope.


### Concrete and Steel


Grouting base plates, concrete pumping, embeds, and anchor bolts are common omissions. Civil, structural, and architectural drawings sometimes conflict on these items. That conflict needs to be resolved before award — not as an RFI in month three.


### Drywall and Interiors


Wall blocking, insulation within drywall assemblies, hollow metal door frames, and gypcrete are frequently excluded in sub bids without clear callout. Review against the spec section and the drawings — not just the sub's exclusion list.

## The Eight Habits That Prevent Scope Gaps at Award


Provision's research identified eight consistent habits among the GC procurement teams with the best scope outcomes. Here are the four most relevant to pre-award review:


1. **Drawings-first, not boilerplate-first.** Start every scope package from the current drawing set. Templates are a floor, not a starting point.
2. **Specific document references.** "See Section 07 54 00, Sheet A-201" is enforceable. "As per plans and specs" is not.
3. **Front-load the buyout conversations.** The pre-bid walk is a scoping tool. Use it to confirm trade coverage before bids are received.
4. **The pre-issue scope review checkpoint.** Before a scope goes to subs, one person reviews it against the full document set. Not the estimator who wrote it.

## Procurement Is the Last Line Before the Field

Pre-award is the moment procurement has maximum leverage. The subcontract isn't signed. Scope can still be defined, questioned, and confirmed without a change order.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is construction procurement subcontractor scope vetting?


It's the process of reviewing subcontractor bids before award to confirm that every required scope item is covered, exclusions are documented, and the sub's price aligns to the project's actual scope of work. Done correctly, it prevents change orders and disputes during construction.


### When should scope vetting happen in the procurement process?


Before the subcontract is signed. Pre-award is the window where scope can be confirmed, questioned, and assigned without cost. Once the subcontract executes, unresolved gaps typically become change orders — and the leverage to resolve them cheaply is gone.


### What are the most common scope gaps in subcontractor bids?


MEP specialty items (motor starters, fire-rated louvres, generator conditioning), envelope transitions (roof cover board, masonry flashings), and concrete work items (pumping, base plate grouting) appear most frequently. These items often sit in multiple spec sections and fall between trades.


### How does AI help with pre-award scope review?


Purpose-built construction AI like Provision's[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) reads the full project set — drawings, specifications, contracts, and addenda — and generates a trade-by-trade scope package in under 60 minutes. It links every item to its source document, giving procurement a verified baseline to compare sub bids against.


### What's the risk of relying on "as per plans and specs" in subcontract scope?


It's the most common anti-pattern in pre-construction. The phrase sounds complete but confirms nothing. When a dispute arises, each party interprets the documents differently. Specific section and drawing references are enforceable. Generic incorporation language is not.


### How accurate is AI-generated scope extraction compared to manual review?


Provision's Scope Agent achieves 97% match accuracy on scope item extraction. The human estimator baseline on the same exercise is 91.3% — at approximately four days per project. The AI doesn't replace estimator judgment, but it dramatically reduces the manual load and catches items that time pressure causes humans to miss.
